n: Paul asks the saints to see their leaders correctly: as servants of Christ and as stewards entrusted with God’s revealed truths — not as celebrities.

f.g: Household managers who care for a master’s property, accountable to him.

n: The one thing required of a steward is faithfulness to the master who appointed him.
Paul isn’t worried about how the Corinthians or any human court rates him. He doesn’t even make himself the final judge of his own service.

f.g: Literally “man’s day” — a human court’s verdict, in contrast to the Lord’s day of judgment.

n: Paul’s conscience is clear, but that doesn’t prove he is innocent. Only the Lord’s judgment counts.

f.g: I am not aware of any wrongdoing on my part.

n: So don’t pass final judgment on anyone before the Lord comes. He will bring hidden things to light and reveal people’s motives, and each faithful person will receive praise from God.
Paul used himself and Apollos as an example so the saints would learn not to go beyond what scripture teaches and not to puff themselves up by favoring one leader over another.

f.g: Inflated with pride, like a bellows.

n: Paul deflates their pride: who made you special? Every gift you have was given to you. Why brag as if you earned it?

f.w: what hast thou that thou didst not receive?

n: With biting irony Paul says: You think you’ve already arrived — full, rich, ruling like kings — without us! I wish you really did reign, so we could share it.

f.g: Some Corinthians seemed to think they had already reached full spiritual glory.

n: Meanwhile the apostles are treated like condemned prisoners paraded last in a Roman victory march or arena, a spectacle for the world, angels, and people to stare at.

f.g: Greek theatron — a show in a theater or arena.

n: More irony: the apostles are fools, weak, and despised for Christ, while the Corinthians imagine themselves wise, strong, and honored.
Paul describes his real life as a missionary: hungry, thirsty, poorly clothed, beaten, and homeless.
He worked with his own hands to support himself. When insulted, he blessed; when persecuted, he endured — just as Jesus taught.
When slandered, they answered kindly. The world treated them like garbage, the scrapings everyone throws out.

f.g: Dirt scraped off; the lowest scum.

n: Paul’s tone softens. He isn’t trying to humiliate them; he warns them as a loving father warns his children.
They might have countless tutors in the faith, but only one spiritual father — Paul, who brought them to Christ through the gospel.

f.g: Greek paidagogos — a guardian who escorted children; a tutor, not a parent.

n: So he urges them to follow his example of humble discipleship.
That’s why Paul sent Timothy, his faithful “son” in the gospel, to remind them of Paul’s Christlike way of life — the same thing he teaches in every church.
Some arrogant members were acting as if Paul would never come back to hold them accountable.
Paul plans to come soon, God willing, and he will test not their talk but their actual spiritual power.
God’s kingdom isn’t a matter of impressive words but of real power — changed lives and the Spirit at work.

f.w: not in word, but in power

n: Paul gives them a choice: should he come with a rod of discipline, or with love and gentleness? Their repentance will decide.
